records.place: Figari, Corse Figari, in the far south of Corsica

wine.name: Corse Figari Rouge
wine.grapes: Niellucciu, about four fifths in the vintages the merchants describe, with Sciaccarellu, Syrah and, in some years, Carcaghjolu Neru for the rest; the blend moves with the year.
wine.sites: The estate's vineyards outside Figari, on granite in an open, dry and windswept corner of the island's far south, where cork oak, olive and maquis grow beside the vines.
wine.making: The red spends well over a year in oak, by the merchants' accounts, which do not agree on the casks: large foudres for fourteen to eighteen months in one account, barrels in others. The vines are farmed biodynamically, certified since 2006, and the clay jars of the house are kept for its separate Amphora red.
wine.glass: Blackberry, sloe and bramble over sap, cracked pepper and the dried herbs of the maquis; sweetly fruited yet fresh and medium in body, with fine, firm tannin and a salty finish.
wine.ageing: Generous within two or three years of the vintage, it holds and gains in savour for several years more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; if a young bottle seems tight, decant it for an hour; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The regional appellation Corse, or Vin de Corse, with the name of Figari, one of its five named zones.
The Corsican name for Nielluccio, the grape DNA ties to Sangiovese, the larger part of this red in the vintages described.

records.table: Granite and wind shape Clos Canarelli's Corse Figari Rouge, from biodynamic vines in Corsica's far south: mostly Niellucciu, with Sciaccarellu and Syrah, raised in oak for over a year. Bramble fruit and cracked pepper give it freshness and grip.
records.story: Far in the south of Corsica, between Sartène and Bonifacio, the windswept granite plateau of Figari is home to Clos Canarelli, a family estate. By the merchants' accounts and a producer history it was founded in 1968, and in the early 1990s the son of the family took over his father's vines outside Figari. He chose to work with the island's own grapes and without synthetic chemicals in the vineyard: the estate has been farmed organically since 2002 and was certified biodynamic in 2006. He also replanted old Corsican varieties that had nearly disappeared, among them Biancu Gentile, a white, and Carcaghjolu Neru, a red, and bottled some of them apart, outside the appellation. The Corse Figari Rouge is the house's classic red: mostly Niellucciu, with Sciaccarellu, Syrah and in some years Carcaghjolu Neru, raised in oak for well over a year. Granite Corsica is not only pale Sciaccarellu: Figari, one of the five named zones of Vin de Corse, gives here a red of grip and freshness from a dry, wind beaten land.

traps: Clos Canarelli's Figari red is led by Niellucciu in the vintages the merchants describe, not by Sciaccarellu, though the granite south is Sciaccarellu country.
Corse Figari is a named zone of the regional appellation Corse, or Vin de Corse, not a separate appellation as Ajaccio and Patrimonio are.
Niellucciu is Sangiovese under its Corsican name, not Nebbiolo, whatever the sound of the word.

report: The library's Figari Rouge reads Sciaccarellu with Nielluccio; iDealwine and a merchant give about four fifths Niellucciu with Sciaccarellu, Syrah and some Carcaghjolu Neru, and the American importer's pages (not cited: the address carries a living name) give the same for 2017 and 2020 but Sciaccarellu ahead for 2022, so a refuter may want the blend told as moving.
Founded 1968 rests on iDealwine, a restaurant's producer history and the importer's sheet; the son's takeover is 1993 in two accounts and 1992 in one, so the story says the early 1990s.

The casks differ by source: foudres of fourteen to eighteen months (Clos des Spiritueux and the importer), tank and 500 litre barrels (Vins et Millésimes), sixteen months in barrel for the 2023 (iDealwine), so the record says oak for well over a year.
No estate site was reached and the record has no primary source; the importer's host refused the one fetch tried, and the importer, whose name is a living person's, is never cited.

Left out for want of a second citable source: the hamlet of Tarrabucetta, the decomposed granite, the destemming and daily punching down, the Bonifacio limestone vines, Tarra d'Orasi's very old vines, the year the Biancu Gentile was planted, and iDealwine's line that Amphora is the house's flagship.

records.place: Patrimonio, in the Nebbio above the Gulf of Saint-Florent, northern Corsica

wine.name: Patrimonio Carco Blanc
wine.grapes: Vermentinu alone, the Corsican name for Vermentino.
wine.sites: Carco, an east facing slope of limestone near the sea at Patrimonio, planted with Vermentinu by the family in 1987.
wine.making: Vermentinu from the one parcel, farmed organically, made by the father after the estate was shared and bottled as Patrimonio Blanc under the family label. The accounts read give no vessel or length of élevage for Carco alone, so none is given here.
wine.glass: Ripe pear and sage over a salty, chalky edge, with a hint of blood orange peel; full and opulent for a Vermentino, yet fresh, with a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: On release it is generous; it gains in depth for several years in bottle, and a good vintage keeps well beyond them.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool rather than cold; no need to decant, though air helps a young bottle; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The appellation of the Nebbio, recognised by the decree of 13 March 1968, the first on Corsica; its white is Vermentinu.

records.table: By the sea at Patrimonio, on a limestone slope the family planted in 1987, grows the Vermentinu of Carco, Domaine Antoine Arena's white. Full, salty and long, with pear and sage, it shows how Corsican Vermentino can age.
records.story: Law in Nice came first for the man whose name the domaine carries: a son of a Patrimonio family, he came home to the family vines in the middle of the 1970s. The appellation itself was young: Patrimonio had been recognised by the decree of 13 March 1968, the first on Corsica, for its pocket of limestone in the Nebbio. The family vines have long been farmed organically. In 1987 the family planted Vermentinu on an east facing limestone slope near the sea; that parcel, Carco, gave the white that carries its name. Ten years later, in 1997, he and a few fellow growers took cuttings of Biancu Gentile, an old island white close to vanishing, and replanted it, and the family later bottled it as Vin de France. Around 2014 the estate was shared: each of the two sons took parcels and began to bottle under his own name, while the parents kept a share and the father went on making a few wines under the family label, Carco among them. Carco argues for Corsican Vermentino from limestone: a white of weight and salt that can live for years.

records.place: Casalabriva in the Taravo valley, Corse-du-Sud, Corsica

wine.name: Cuvée Faustine Rouge
wine.grapes: Sciaccarellu, about seven tenths, with Niellucciu for the rest, by the estate's own sheet.
wine.sites: Hillsides of granite sand in the Taravo valley of southern Corsica, at about 150 metres, farmed biodynamically for more than twenty years by the estate's account.
wine.making: Brought in by gravity, the grapes are destemmed but not crushed and stay about a month on their skins in concrete vats, pumped over daily, the fermentations starting on their own. After pressing the wine spends six months in stainless steel tank and is blended, racked and lightly filtered, then bottled.
wine.glass: Cherry red with ruby lights; red cherry, myrtle berry and cracked pepper over the scent of the maquis; light in body and fresh, with fine, silky tannin.
wine.ageing: Ready within its first year, it keeps for several years when the year is good, the fruit softening into something more savoury.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, a little cool, with no decanting; a Burgundy glass suits its perfume.

label.means: The national category for wine outside the appellation rules; the house took all its wines out of the appellations.

records.table: Labelled Vin de France, Domaine Comte Abbatucci's Cuvée Faustine Rouge comes from the granite of the Taravo valley: Sciaccarellu with some Niellucciu, fermented on its own yeasts in concrete and kept six months in steel. Pale and peppery, scented with myrtle, it goes to the table a little cool.
records.story: Historic figures of the Abbatuccis, an old family of southern Corsica, give the Collection wines their names, as the house tells it: a minister of the Empire, a general of the French Revolution, a diplomat. By the listing of Vins de Corse, the island's wine body, the vineyard in the Taravo valley was planted in 1950. In the 1960s the head of the estate, alarmed that the island's old grapes were disappearing, took cuttings from threatened vineyards and planted some eighteen native varieties side by side on one granite hillside; by the wine body's account the estate became the island's first ampelographic station. His son took the estate on in 1992, carried the work on and turned it to biodynamic farming in 2000. The old grapes went first into the Cuvées Collection, bottled as Vin de France because the appellation rules left little room for them; a few years later the house took all its wines out of the appellations, and Faustine, named for a daughter of the family, has since carried the words Vin de France. The red is Sciaccarellu with some Niellucciu from granite, made without oak. Faustine pours the pale, peppery red of the Ajaccio country, a reminder that a Vin de France label can hold a wine of a place.

records.place: Rogliano, at the northern tip of Cap Corse, Corsica

wine.name: Muscatellu, Muscat du Cap Corse
wine.grapes: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains alone, the one grape of the appellation.
wine.sites: Steep schist slopes and narrow terraces at Rogliano, almost at the sea's edge on the northern tip of Cap Corse, beaten by strong winds.
wine.making: About half the crop, by the island wine body's listing, is left to shrivel before pressing, on the vine by the Hachette guide's notes, as the cape has long done. As for every Muscat du Cap Corse, neutral grape spirit is then added during fermentation, the mutage, which stops the yeast and keeps the grape's sugar.
wine.glass: Candied apricot, honey and orange blossom with orange zest and a touch of saffron; sweet and rich, yet fresh, with a clean, lingering finish; with age, raisin, hazelnut and beeswax.
wine.ageing: Perfumed and open young, it ages for many years in bottle towards raisin, hazelnut and beeswax.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass, as an aperitif or with fiadone, the island's brocciu cheesecake.

label.means: The vin doux naturel appellation of Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, from seventeen communes of Cap Corse and the Patrimonio country.
The name the house gives its Muscat du Cap Corse.

records.table: Rogliano, at the northern tip of Corsica, gives Clos Nicrosi the schist terraces above the sea for Muscatellu, its Muscat du Cap Corse. Grapes partly shrivelled and a fermentation stopped with grape spirit give honey, candied apricot and orange blossom; pour it chilled as an aperitif or with fiadone.
records.story: Small vineyards cling to steep schist above the sea at Rogliano, near the tip of Cap Corse, the narrow peninsula that points north towards the Ligurian coast. Clos Nicrosi was founded there in 1850 by a forebear of the family, whose name the estate keeps. A century later the vineyard was taken up again: in 1959 the founder's descendants restored it on its terraces above the sea, and the same family has made its wine ever since. The house's reputation rests on two wines, a dry white under Corse Coteaux du Cap Corse and the Muscat it calls Muscatellu. For the Muscat the family keeps an old habit of the cape: about half the grapes are left to shrivel before pressing, and spirit is then added to stop the fermentation. Muscat du Cap Corse became an appellation of its own in the 1990s, drawn from seventeen communes of the cape and the Patrimonio country and given to Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains alone. Muscatellu holds the island's sweet wine in its classic form: Muscat from schist by the sea, rich yet fresh, the sweet answer to the island's dry Vermentino.

cards.back: Muscat à Petits Grains from schist at Rogliano, part of it dried, with grape spirit added during fermentation.

cards.front: When was Clos Nicrosi founded at Rogliano, and when was its vineyard restored?

questions.q: How does Clos Nicrosi's Muscatellu keep its sweetness?
opts: Grape spirit is added during fermentation
The grapes are picked frozen on the vine
Noble rot concentrates the berries
Sweet grape juice is added before bottling
questions.exp: As a vin doux naturel it is stopped with neutral grape spirit, the mutage; part of the crop is also dried first, but that is neither noble rot nor ice wine.

questions.q: Clos Nicrosi was founded at Rogliano in 1850. What happened to its vineyard in 1959?
opts: The founder's descendants restored it
It was sold to a co-operative of the cape
It was replanted with Sciaccarellu
It became the first Corsican appellation
questions.exp: A century after the founding, the founder's descendants took up and restored the vineyard; Patrimonio, not Rogliano, was the first Corsican appellation, in 1968.

report: The plan's note is answered: the Muscat is labelled Muscatellu, Muscat du Cap Corse, in the Hachette guide and iDealwine, and the Wine Scholar Guild calls it the house's flagship, so the pick stands and the dry Coteaux du Cap Corse white goes in others.

Founded 1850 and the restoration of 1959 rest on the Vins de Corse listing and the Hachette guide; the founder, Dominique Nicrosi, and the two Luigi brothers who restored the vineyard could not be dated, so they are described, not named.

The region record dates Muscat du Cap Corse to 1993; the INAO's own Rivesaltes page lists 26 March 1993, but an INAO committee report of 2017 gives initial recognition by the decree of 19 November 1997, so the story says the 1990s and the region record should be read again.
The drying rests on the Hachette guide's notes across several vintages and a merchant; the share dried, about half by one account, is left out.
Left out for want of a source: the white's grape (Vermentinu by the plan and the region's whites, not named by the sources read), the estate's organic conversion, and the alcohol of the Muscat.
Living names for people.json, never in the fragment: Jean-Noël Luigi, Marine Luigi, Sébastien Luigi.
Searches for this record: 4 of the group's 35.

changed: wine.making: "Part of the crop is left to dry before pressing, on the vine or in crates in the September sun, and in older vintages on slabs of stone, as the cape once did."; now "About half the crop, by the island wine body's listing, is left to shrivel before pressing, on the vine by the Hachette guide's notes, as the cape has long done.": The wine body's listing gives the Muscat as half the crop dried and the Hachette guide's notes of the 2012 and the 2021 give the grapes shrivelled on the vine before the mutage; neither gives crates or slabs of stone.

story: "part of the grapes are dried before pressing, once on slabs of stone, in later years on the vine or in crates in the September sun, and spirit"; now "about half the grapes are left to shrivel before pressing, and spirit": As in the making.

others.0.note: "The estate's dry white from the cape's schist, rich and powerful, raised in tank."; now "The estate's dry white from the cape's schist, rich and powerful by the Hachette guide's notes.": The tank rests on one guide's note and no second source; the description is the guide's and is hedged so.
open: The first recognition of Muscat du Cap Corse is 1997 in the INAO's commission report of 2017 and 1993 in the region record and the author's reading of another INAO page; a cross reference table of the INAO even gives 1949. The story says the 1990s; the region record should be read again.
Serving: iDealwine suggests 12 degrees for the 2017; the record keeps the Codex's 6 to 8 for sweet whites.

records.place: Poggio d'Oletta, Patrimonio, in the Nebbio of northern Corsica

wine.name: Petra Bianca, Patrimonio Rouge
wine.grapes: Niellucciu alone, the Corsican name for Nielluccio, the grape DNA ties to Sangiovese.
wine.sites: The Petra Bianca parcel at Poggio d'Oletta, on the clay and limestone that set the Patrimonio country apart from the island's granite and schist.
wine.making: From vines farmed organically, by the merchants' accounts. The Niellucciu is fermented and then raised in stainless steel vats, with no wood, for eighteen months to two years by vintage, by a merchant's sheet and a restaurant's list, which keeps its fruit clear and its tannin fine.
wine.glass: Ripe red and black cherry with menthol, a light floral lift and dried maquis herbs; deeply coloured, precise rather than heavy, with firm, fine grained tannin and lively acidity.
wine.ageing: A few years in bottle reward its firm, rather closed youth, and it holds for several years after, its flavours filling out.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; give a young bottle an hour's decanting; a Burgundy glass or a large red wine glass.

label.means: The Nebbio appellation recognised by the decree of 13 March 1968, the first on Corsica, its reds led by Niellucciu.
The name of the estate's parcel at Poggio d'Oletta, which gives the wine its name.

records.table: In steel vats, never wood, Domaine Leccia raises Petra Bianca, its Patrimonio Rouge of Niellucciu alone, the Corsican Sangiovese, from the clay and limestone of Poggio d'Oletta. Cherry and menthol over firm, fine tannin call for lamb or wild boar.
records.story: The Leccias made vines their main business around 1900, by the accounts read, at Poggio d'Oletta, a hill village of the Nebbio above the Gulf of Saint-Florent. Patrimonio, recognised by the decree of 13 March 1968, became the first appellation of Corsica, and the family's Niellucciu grew on the pocket of limestone and clay that sets it apart from the rest of the island. A brother and sister ran the estate together for many years; in 2004 or 2005, as the accounts differ, the brother left to found his own domaine, E Croce, in the same village, and the sister kept the family estate and its cellar, and later turned it to organic farming. In the middle of the 2010s the brother's son took on the work of the family domaine, in 2014 or 2016 by his importer's two accounts, beside his aunt. Its Petra Bianca, a red named for its parcel, is Niellucciu alone from clay and limestone, raised in steel rather than oak. It shows the appellation's rule and its grape at once: Patrimonio red as Sangiovese speaks it on Corsican limestone, deep and firm when young and better for a few years in bottle.

Niellucciu, Petra Bianca's one grape, is tied by DNA to Sangiovese; the likeness of its name to Nebbiolo misleads.
Petra Bianca on this label is a parcel of Patrimonio; Domaine de Petra Bianca is a different estate, in Figari in the far south.

cards.back: Niellucciu alone, from clay and limestone at Poggio d'Oletta in the Patrimonio country.

cards.front: Which domaine did the brother of the Leccia family found apart in 2004 or 2005?
cards.back: Domaine d'E Croce, in the same village of Poggio d'Oletta.

questions.q: A guest wants a Corsican red close in grape to Chianti. Why does Domaine Leccia's Petra Bianca fit?
opts: It is Niellucciu alone, the Corsican Sangiovese
It is Sciaccarellu, the Corsican Mammolo
It is Nebbiolo grown on Corsican limestone
It blends Grenache and Syrah from the plain
questions.exp: Petra Bianca is Niellucciu alone, a grape DNA ties to Sangiovese, Chianti's grape; despite its name Niellucciu is not Nebbiolo.

questions.q: What changed at the Leccia family estate of Poggio d'Oletta in 2004 or 2005?

The estate was sold to a Bastia merchant
It joined the Patrimonio co-operative
Its vines were moved to the eastern plain
questions.exp: The brother and sister had run it together; he founded E Croce in the same village and she kept Domaine Leccia, where the brother's son later took on the work.

report: The plan's note is answered: the red is Petra Bianca, Niellucciu alone, in the Hachette guide and two merchants, and Domaine Leccia is the family estate, not Domaine d'E Croce, which the brother founded apart.
Founded is left empty: two accounts give the turn of the twentieth century, around 1900, and none gives a year.

The brother's leaving is 2005 in the Hachette guide and 2004 in the importer's portfolio, and the nephew's taking on the work 2014 in the importer's article and 2016 in its portfolio; a Visit Corsica interview confirms the nephew's part but its address carries living names, so it is not cited, and the story gives both years for each.

The stainless steel vats rest on Cavesa (24 months for the 2021) and a restaurant's list (18 or 24 months by vintage); Hachette's note of the 2007 adds that it was made without added yeasts, from that guide alone, so it is left out.

The closed youth and the two years of waiting rest on the Hachette guide's note of the 2007 and the region record's line that Patrimonio reds are made to age a few years, so the record says a few years.

Left out for want of a second source: the generation that began estate bottling in the 1950s, the organic certification year (2005, 2007, 2008 and 2011 in different accounts), the age of the vines and the hectares; the estate's own site was seen only on a rosé page served without https, so it is not cited.
Living names for people.json, never in the fragment: Annette Leccia, Yves Leccia, Lisandru Leccia, Sandrine Leccia.
Searches for this record: 8 of the group's 35, with the INAO search on Patrimonio shared with Domaine Antoine Arena; all 35 of the share were spent.

changed: wine.making: "From vines farmed organically since the estate's conversion in the 2000s."; now "From vines farmed organically, by the merchants' accounts.": The certification is 2005, 2007, 2008 or 2011 by account and the importer once described the estate as in conversion, so no decade is said; organic stands on Cavesa and the importer.

wine.making: "for eighteen months to two years by a merchant's sheet"; now "for eighteen months to two years by vintage, by a merchant's sheet": Cavesa gives 24 months for the 2021, the Hachette guide two years for a 2011 red and another listing 18 months for a 2020 red: the length moves by vintage.

story: "and the sister kept the family estate, which she turned to organic farming in the 2000s."; now "and the sister kept the family estate and its cellar, and later turned it to organic farming.": The Hachette guide records that she kept part of the vineyard and the cellar when the brother left; the decade of the organic turn is not settled, as in the making.

story: "The red the house is known by is Petra Bianca, named for its parcel: Niellucciu alone"; now "Its Petra Bianca, a red named for its parcel, is Niellucciu alone": Cavesa lists three Patrimonio reds of the estate (Patrimonio Rouge, Petra Bianca and Pettale), so no source of the refuter's makes Petra Bianca the one red the house is known by.
open: Petra Bianca is one of three Patrimonio reds of the estate; the plan's Patrimonio Rouge may mean the estate's plain Patrimonio Rouge rather than Petra Bianca. The pick is kept (the plan's note names Petra Bianca and the importer calls its parcel the estate's own), for the read-together agent.
The eighteen months for a 2020 red may be the plain Patrimonio Rouge rather than Petra Bianca; the record says eighteen months to two years by vintage.
The brother's son taking on the work in 2014 or 2016 rests on the importer's two accounts as the author read them; the refuter met the role, not the year.
